Presenters without the boilerplate: the life cycle step by step

What runs between a request and a rendered page, where to load data, where to check permissions and why a signal comes before the render.

JNJan Novák 2 days ago Nette

A presenter in Nette is a class that answers one request. It looks simple until a page has a form, a table with AJAX and a check of permissions at once. Then it matters in which order its methods run, because each of them has its job.

The order of the methods

Every request goes through the same steps. A method that is missing is skipped, so a small presenter can have only one of them.

  1. startup() runs first: the place for a check that applies to the whole presenter, such as a signed-in user.
  2. action<Name>() decides what happens: it loads the record, redirects when it does not exist, changes the view.
  3. handle<Signal>() processes a signal: a click on a link with ! or a submitted form of a component.
  4. beforeRender() prepares what every template needs, the menu for example.
  5. render<Name>() passes the data to the template.

Load in the action, show in the render

A common mistake is to load a record in render. A signal runs before it, so a handler that needs the record has nothing to work with. Load it in the action and keep it in a property:

// the record is loaded once, for the signals and for the render
public function actionDetail(string $slug): void
{
	$this->article = $this->articles->getBySlug($slug)
		?? $this->error('Article not found');
}

public function renderDetail(): void
{
	$this->template->article = $this->article;
}

The action decides, the render shows. Everything between them can rely on the data being there.

Where the permissions belong

A check in startup() covers pages and signals alike, which a check in the template never does: a hidden button still has an address that can be called. In Drago every presenter has its resource and each signal its own privilege, so a role can read a page and still not delete from it.

The button in the template is hidden for the same privilege, so nobody sees what they may not use:

{if $user->isAllowed('Backend:Blog', 'delete')}
	<a n:href="delete! $article->id" class="btn btn-danger">Delete</a>
{/if}

What to take away

  • Decide in the action, show in the render.
  • Check permissions in startup() or by an attribute, never only in the template.
  • After a signal redirect, or redraw a snippet when the request is AJAX.

With these three rules a presenter stays short, and a new signal or form is a few lines that do not change the rest.
